core.text: 3 Methodology

The overall framework of our proposed Guided Verifier pipeline is illustrated in Figure 2. We formulate multimodal reasoning as a collaborative process rather than an unguided exploration. Our pipeline consists of three distinct phases: (1) CoRe Data Synthesis Pipeline (Section 3.2), where we construct a specialized dataset of reasoning trajectories with dense hallucination annotations; (2) Guided Verifier SFT (Section 3.3), where a lightweight verifier is trained to detect inconsistencies and provide corrective guidance; and (3) Guided-GRPO (Section 3.4), where the policy model is optimized via Guided-GRPO mechanism.
3.1 Preliminaries

Task Definition. We consider a multimodal reasoning task where the input consists of a visual context vv and a textual query qq, denoted jointly as x=(v,q)x=(v,q). The goal is to generate a multi-step reasoning chain y=(o1,o2,…,oT)y=(o_{1},o_{2},\dots,o_{T}) that leads to a correct final answer, where each oto_{t} represents a reasoning step. Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote the multimodal policy model parameterized by θ\theta. In standard autoregressive generation, the joint probability of the trajectory is factorized as:
pθ​(y|x)=∏t=1Tπθ​(ot|x,o<t)p_{\theta}(y|x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{\theta}(o_{t}|x,o_{<t}) (1)
where o<to_{<t} denotes the history of generated steps.

Standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To align the policy with human preferences or logical correctness, RL is typically employed. GRPO [24] serves as a efficient baseline by eliminating the need for a parametric value function. For each input xx, GRPO samples a group of GG outputs {yi}i=1G\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the old policy πθo​l​d\pi_{\theta_{old}}. The optimization objective is defined as:

𝒥G​R​P​O​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{GRPO}(\theta) =𝔼x∼𝒟,{yi}i=1G∼πθo​l​d[1G∑i=1G1|yi|∑t=1|yi|\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{old}}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|y_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|} (2) min⁡(πθ​(ot,i|x,o<t,i)πθo​l​d​(ot,i|x,o<t,i)​Ai,clip​(…)​Ai)\displaystyle\min\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{t,i}|x,o_{<t,i})}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(o_{t,i}|x,o_{<t,i})}A_{i},\text{clip}(\dots)A_{i}\right) −β𝔻K​L],\displaystyle-\beta\mathbb{D}_{KL}\Bigg],

where the clipping term follows the standard PPO formulation, i.e., clip⁡(rt,i, 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ)\mathrm{clip}(r_{t,i},\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon), with rt,i=πθ​(ot,i∣x,o<t,i)/πθold​(ot,i∣x,o<t,i)r_{t,i}=\pi_{\theta}(o_{t,i}\mid x,o_{<t,i})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{t,i}\mid x,o_{<t,i}).
Crucially, the advantage AiA_{i} for the ii-th trajectory is computed using group-relative statistics rather than a value network prediction:
Ai=ri−mean​({rj}j=1G)std​({rj}j=1G)+ϵ,A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\text{mean}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\text{std}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})+\epsilon}, (3)

where rir_{i} is the terminal reward for trajectory yiy_{i}. Note that standard GRPO relies on sparse, delayed feedback (rir_{i} is only available at step TT) and assumes an open-loop rollout where πθ\pi_{\theta} operates in isolation.

Dual-Model Collaborative Inference. To address the error propagation inherent in open-loop reasoning, we redefine the generation process as a dual-agent interaction between the Policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and a Guided Verifier VϕV_{\phi}. At each step tt, the verifier observes the current reasoning step oto_{t} and produces a guidance signal gtg_{t}. The policy’s transition probability is thus conditioned on this dynamic guidance:
pguided​(y|x)=∏t=1Tπθ​(ot|x,o<t,g<t),p_{\text{guided}}(y|x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{\theta}(o_{t}|x,o_{<t},g_{<t}), (4)
where g<tg_{<t} represents the history of verification signals, effectively transforming the rollout into a closed-loop control system where the verifier actively steers the trajectory.
3.2 Stage1: CoRe Data Synthesis Pipeline

We construct a supervised multimodal math dialogue dataset for guided verifier training. Unlike standard instruction-tuning data that focuses only on correct outcomes, our pipeline explicitly captures process negatives: intermediate steps that deviate logically but are guided back to the correct trajectory within the same dialogue.

Automated Dialogue Generation. We simulate multi-turn interactions between a Guide (verifier) and a Solver (user) under a guide-and-correction protocol. To ensure ground-truth-aligned final answers and reduce stochastic artifacts, we decode with temperature 00.

Sampling-based Step-wise Hallucination Scoring. For each Solver response, we use GPT-4o [21] as an oracle evaluator to assign a binary validity label (11 for logically consistent, 00 for hallucinated) via N=10N=10 independent sampling trials. Let s¯\bar{s} be the average score; we derive the final label with a dual-threshold rule:
S={1if ​s¯≥0.70if ​s¯≤0.3DiscardotherwiseS=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\bar{s}\geq 0.7\\ 0&\text{if }\bar{s}\leq 0.3\\ \text{Discard}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (5)
This high-confidence labeling mitigates ambiguous cases while providing dense supervision over intermediate reasoning steps.

Filtering and Output. We apply three filters for training stability: (i) pruning trajectories exceeding 28k tokens, (ii) discarding trajectories whose hallucination-step ratio exceeds 15%, and (iii) enforcing strict stop-format integrity so that dialogues terminate only after a valid final answer is produced. The resulting dataset CoRe contains 2,792 trajectories and 26,360 step-wise supervision signals, with 24,946 positives and 1,406 negatives. Appendix 9 provides the dataset’s detailed statistics.
3.3 Stage2: Guided Verifier SFT

The objective of this stage is to instill the specialized capability of discriminative verification into a multimodal generator. We utilize the high-quality dataset constructed in Stage 1 to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [4], parameterized by ϕ\phi, transforming it into the Guided Verifier VϕV_{\phi}.

Input-Output Formulation. We formulate the verification task as a conditional generation problem following the standard instruction-tuning paradigm. The input consists of the multimodal context (image vv and query qq) and a specific reasoning step oto_{t} generated by the policy. We structure the data into the ShareGPT [7] format, where the verifier acts as an assistant evaluating the user’s provided step. Formally, for a given trajectory step, the input prompt is denoted as ℐ=(v,q,o<t,ot)\mathcal{I}=(v,q,o_{<t},o_{t}), and the target output is the verification signal gtg_{t} (i.e., the guidance tokens together with hallucination score).
Training Objective. We employ standard SFT to optimize the verifier. The model is trained to minimize the autoregressive cross-entropy loss over the target tokens of the verification signal:

ℒS​F​T​(ϕ)=−𝔼(ℐ,gt)∼𝒟v​e​r​[∑k=1|gt|log⁡Pϕ​(gt,k∣ℐ,gt,<k)]\mathcal{L}_{SFT}(\phi)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\mathcal{I},g_{t})\sim\mathcal{D}_{ver}}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{|g_{t}|}\log P_{\phi}(g_{t,k}\mid\mathcal{I},g_{t,<k})\right] (6)

where gt,kg_{t,k} denotes the kk-th token of the verification output. We utilize the LLaMA-Factory framework [35] for efficient implementation. Through this process, the verifier learns to map reasoning patterns to explicit validity scores, establishing the discriminative foundation required for the subsequent RL phase.
3.4 Stage3: Guided-GRPO

In the final stage, we freeze the guided verifier VϕV_{\phi} obtained from Stage 2 and employ it as a dynamic environmental agent to assist the policy model πθ\pi_{\theta}. We formulate the reasoning process as a sequential decision-making problem where the state space is iteratively augmented by verification signals.

Guided Rollout Dynamics. We design a dual-view interaction mechanism where the Policy and Verifier operate with distinct system prompts and context windows. Let 𝒫s​y​sπ\mathcal{P}_{sys}^{\pi} and 𝒫s​y​sV\mathcal{P}_{sys}^{V} denote the system prompts for the policy and verifier, respectively. Recall that the input xx consists of the visual context vv and textual query qq. The rollout proceeds iteratively:

Reasoning Phase (Policy Step): At step tt, the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} generates the reasoning segment oto_{t}. To provide focused correction without context pollution, the policy’s input ℐtπ\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\pi} includes the full reasoning history but appends only the most recent guidance signal gt−1g_{t-1} from the previous turn:
ℐtπ=𝒫s​y​sπ⊕v⊕q⏟x⊕o<t⊕𝒯⁡(gt−1)\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\pi}=\mathcal{P}_{sys}^{\pi}\oplus\underbrace{v\oplus q}_{x}\oplus o_{<t}\oplus\mathcal{T}(g_{t-1}) (7)

where o<to_{<t} represents the concatenation of all prior reasoning steps, and 𝒯⁡(gt−1)\mathcal{T}(g_{t-1}) applies the formatting template to the latest verifier feedback (with g0=∅g_{0}=\emptyset). The step is sampled as ot∼πθ(⋅|ℐtπ)o_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\pi}).

Verification Phase (Verifier Step): Upon generating oto_{t}, the frozen verifier VϕV_{\phi} inspects the trajectory. The verifier’s context ℐtV\mathcal{I}_{t}^{V} aggregates the original input and the cumulative reasoning chain up to the current step:
ℐtV=𝒫s​y​sV⊕v⊕q⏟x⊕o≤t\mathcal{I}_{t}^{V}=\mathcal{P}_{sys}^{V}\oplus\underbrace{v\oplus q}_{x}\oplus o_{\leq t} (8)
The verifier then outputs the guidance signal gtg_{t} (containing the critique and hallucination score) based on this comprehensive view.

This process repeats until a stop token is generated, resulting in a guided trajectory τ=(o1,g1,o2,g2,…,oT)\tau=(o_{1},g_{1},o_{2},g_{2},\dots,o_{T}). By explicitly embedding gtg_{t} into the context, the verifier effectively prunes the search space, steering the policy away from hallucinated branches in real-time.

Composite Reward Engineering. To ensure holistic optimization, we design a dense reward function R⁡(τ)R(\tau) that aggregates signals from three distinct dimensions. The total reward for a trajectory is a weighted sum:
R⁡(τ)=λa​c​c⋅ra​c​c+λv​e​r⋅rv​e​r+λf​m​t⋅rf​m​tR(\tau)=\lambda_{acc}\cdot r_{acc}+\lambda_{ver}\cdot r_{ver}+\lambda_{fmt}\cdot r_{fmt} (9)
The components are defined as follows:

Correctness Reward (ra​c​cr_{acc}): A binary indicator 𝕀⁡(yp​r​e​d=yg​t)\mathbb{I}(y_{pred}=y_{gt}) reflecting whether the final answer matches the ground truth. This serves as the primary optimization objective (λa​c​c=0.8\lambda_{acc}=0.8).

Hallucination Penalty (rv​e​rr_{ver}): Derived from the verifier’s own judgments during rollout. Let Nf​a​i​lN_{fail} be the count of steps where VϕV_{\phi} detected hallucinations (i.e., score 0). We define rv​e​r=1−Nf​a​i​lTr_{ver}=1-\frac{N_{fail}}{T}, encouraging the policy to minimize verifier-triggered interventions (λv​e​r=0.1\lambda_{ver}=0.1).

Format Compliance (rf​m​tr_{fmt}): To ensure the generated solutions are parseable, we impose strict syntactic constraints. A reward is assigned only if the trajectory concludes with the correct XML encapsulation tags (<answer> … </answer>) and the final result is properly enclosed within LaTeX-style boxing (i.e., \boxed{result}). This rule-based component stabilizes the training by enforcing output structure (λf​m​t=0.1\lambda_{fmt}=0.1).

Group Relative Policy Optimization with Guidance. We adapt the GRPO objective to this guided setting. For each query xx, we sample a group of GG guided trajectories {τi}i=1G\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the current policy interacting with the verifier. The advantage AiA_{i} is computed relative to the group’s composite rewards. The gradient update is performed via:

∇θ𝒥\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J} =𝔼⁡[1G​∑i=1G∑t=1TiAi​min⁡(ρt,clip⁡(ρt,1−ϵ,1+ϵ))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}A_{i}\,\min\Big(\rho_{t},\,\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\Big)\Bigg] (10) −β𝔻KL(πθ∥πref)\displaystyle-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)

where ρt=πθ​(ot,i|𝒞t−1,i)πθo​l​d​(ot,i|𝒞t−1,i)\rho_{t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{t,i}|\mathcal{C}_{t-1,i})}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(o_{t,i}|\mathcal{C}_{t-1,i})} is the importance sampling ratio. Crucially, the advantage AiA_{i} now reflects not just the final outcome, but the quality of the collaborative interaction, penalizing trajectories that required excessive correction from the verifier.

Consider a policy rollout over TT steps with an average intrinsic error probability ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) per step. Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) denote the conditional failure probability of the verifier in detecting an error given that one has occurred. Under the assumption of negligible false rejections, the probability of generating a strictly valid trajectory in the open-loop baseline is Po​p​e​n=(1−ϵ)TP_{open}=(1-\epsilon)^{T}. In contrast, the guided closed-loop framework yields a validity probability of Pg​u​i​d​e​d=(1−ϵ​δ)TP_{guided}=(1-\epsilon\delta)^{T}. Since δ<1\delta<1, the guided mechanism strictly reduces the error accumulation rate. Proof. See Appendix 6.1.

Significance: Theorem 3.1 implies that the guided verifier fundamentally reshapes the optimization landscape. By reducing the effective step-wise error from ϵ\epsilon to ϵ​δ\epsilon\delta, it prevents the exponential decay of valid samples in long-horizon rollouts. This ensures that Guided-GRPO receives a sufficient density of high-quality learning signals even when TT is large, effectively mitigating the sparse reward problem.
We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including discussions on correlated errors and false rejections, in Appendix 6.
3.5 Inference Strategy

During the test phase, we evaluate the model using two distinct protocols. 1) Collaborative Inference. The policy and verifier interact iteratively, maintaining the exact prompt concatenation logic defined in Eq. (7) and Eq. (8). 2) Standalone Inference. To assess the internalization of reasoning capabilities, we deploy the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} in isolation. In this setting, the inference reduces to conventional solitary generation.
4 Experiments

In this section, we empirically validate the Guided Verifier framework. Beyond comparing standard performance metrics, we aim to probe the underlying mechanisms of the proposed paradigm shift. Specifically, we investigate three research questions.
RQ1: Effect of Guided Verifier Workflow. Does the closed-loop guided verification mechanism achieve superior performance.
RQ2: Generalization of Guided Verifier. Is the proposed framework generalizable across different model scales.
RQ3: Effect of CoRe Supervised Dataset. How critical is the specialized Data Synthesis Pipeline for equipping the verifier with effective error-correction capabilities?
RQ4: Efficiency of Guided Verifier. How does the SFT of the verifier impact the RL based training and inference efficiency?
4.1 Experiment Setup

Datasets: CoRe’s source data for Verifier SFT. Geometry-3k for G-GRPO training. All Qwen are VL version. Benchmarks: MathVista, MathVerse and MMMU. Model Initialization: Both the policy and verifier are initialized from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. To validate self-verification, the verifier is fine-tuned solely on our synthesized correction dataset, avoiding reliance on distilled larger models.
4.2 RQ1: Efficacy of the Guided Verifier Workflow

We first investigate the overall effectiveness of the Guided Verifier framework by comparing our Qwen3-VL-8B, trained via G-GRPO, against a comprehensive suite of baselines. As illustrated in Table 1, our method demonstrates a significant performance leap on the MathVerse, MathVista, and MMMU benchmarks, rivaling the performance of GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro. Furthermore, compared to other GRPO methods such as Vision-R1-32B, MMR1-32B, and VL-Rethinker-7B, Guided-GRPO maintains distinct advantages. It introduces a qualitative shift in reasoning reliability, effectively mitigating error propagation.

4.3 RQ2: Generalization Across Model Scales

To verify that the observed gains are not an artifact of a specific parameter scale, we evaluate the scalability of our framework. Table 2 presents a comparative analysis of the Solver-Only inference versus the Guided Verifier inference across 4B and 8B parameter scales. The empirical results indicate robust generalization. Incorporating the guided verifier yields consistent performance boosts regardless of the model size. For instance, on the MathVista dataset, the Qwen3-VL-4B model with guided verification (G.V-Qwen3-4B) achieves an accuracy of 69.40%, significantly outperforming its GRPO baseline (68.75%) and even approaching the performance of the unguided 8B base model. This confirms that the ”Guide-and-Correction" paradigm addresses a fundamental limitation in autoregressive reasoning that is scale-agnostic.
4.4 RQ3: Effectiveness of the CoRe Supervised Dataset

A core premise of this work is that a verifier requires specialized training on process-level negatives, the ability to detect and rectify hallucinations, rather than relying solely on generic reasoning capabilities. We validate the impact of our CoRe dataset by comparing verifiers with and without our specialized SFT. Results in Table 3 demonstrate the decisive role of our synthesized dataset. Our Qwen3-8B (SFT) verifier, trained on our synthesized correction trajectories, outperforms the significantly larger GPT-4o when used as a plug-in verifier (Overall: 51.07% vs. 52.34% on MathVerse is highly competitive, and notably superior to open-source baselines like QVQ-72B at 49.87%).

The performance gap highlights that general model does not equate to the ability required by guided verifier. Without the explicit training on hallucination correction provided by our pipeline, even capable models fail to provide the precise, discriminative signals necessary to steer the policy, confirming that the quality of supervision data is the bottleneck for effective verification.
4.5 RQ4: Inference Efficiency

A potential concern with dual-agent systems is the computational overhead. We investigate whether SFT improves the efficiency of the collaboration. For inference phase, a primary concern with iterative verification is the potential for uncontrolled expansion in token consumption and latency. We analyze the inference overhead in terms of interaction turns and total token usage, as visualized in Figure 4 and Figure 4.

Interaction Turns: We observe that the specialized SFT verifier significantly reduces the number of interaction turns required to reach a correct solution compared to a naive (non-SFT) verifier. As shown in Figure 7, the naive verifier (Qwen3-8B without specialized SFT) often engages in prolonged, circular arguments with the policy, failing to provide decisive termination signals. In contrast, our Guided Verifier typically resolves reasoning paths within 2-3 turns. This indicates that the CoRe dataset successfully teaches the verifier to be decisive, correcting errors promptly or validating correct steps immediately, thereby preventing unnecessary computational loops.

Token Consumption: While the closed-loop paradigm inevitably incurs a higher token cost than the single-turn open-loop baseline, the overhead is efficiently managed. Figure 8 demonstrates that the Guided-GRPO model consumes significantly fewer tokens per successful sample than the Policy + Naive Verifier configuration. Furthermore, when normalized by performance gain (tokens per 1% accuracy improvement), the Guided Verifier workflow proves to be highly efficient. It achieves performance parity with significantly larger models (e.g., QVQ-72B) while utilizing a fraction of the parameter count, suggesting that allocating compute to dynamic verification is more resource-efficient than blindly scaling model parameters.
4.6 Ablation Study

To deconstruct the contributions of each component in our framework, we conduct a detailed ablation study in Table 2. We isolate the gains from three progressive stages: the Policy-Only baseline, the introduction of guided verifier workflow, and the application of G-GRPO training.
Effect of Guided Verifier Inference

Comparing the Policy-Only row with Qwen3-VL-8B + Qwen3-VL-8B, we observe only marginal or negligible gains (e.g., MathVista improves from 67.31% to 69.75%). This suggests that simply coupling two models without specific alignment yields limited benefit, as the naive verifier lacks the intent to correct specific multimodal hallucinations.
Effect of Guided Verifier Inference with CoRe.

Replacing the naive verifier with our SFT-trained verifier (Qwen3-VL-8B + G.V-Qwen3-8B) results in a consistent performance uplift across all metrics. For example, on MathVerse (Overall), accuracy improves to 47.23%. This isolation proves that the capability injected by our SFT dataset, specifically the "Guide-and-Correction" protocol, is the primary driver for enabling effective test-time guidance.
Effect of Guided Verifier Inference with G-GRPO.

The most significant jump occurs when the policy is further trained using our Guided-GRPO objective (Qwen3-VL-8B + G.V-Qwen3-8B under G-GRPO section). MathVista performance peaks at 77.88%. This confirms that while the verifier acts as a powerful inference-time guide, the internalization of these signals via RL training (Section 3.4) is essential for maximizing the model’s reasoning potential.
